title: Bridge Captain: Unity 3D
description: Moving Bridge Captain to Unity let me turn the game from a console-driven bridge interface into a fully 3D narrative space. I built an interactable bridge with crew characters, branching conversations, scripted ship events, character cameras, audio, animations, cutscenes, alerts, and dynamic scene changes. I also created a JSON-driven command/event architecture and live authoring tools so mission content could be assembled from reusable commands rather than hard-coded one scene at a time.

sections.title: From Console Interface to Physical Bridge
paragraphs: The Unity generation changed the basic interaction model of Bridge Captain.
Instead of commanding the ship primarily through a 2D dashboard, the player could physically exist on a fully 3D bridge with crew members positioned around the room.

sections.title: Fully 3D Bridge
paragraphs: I prototyped the bridge geometry in Unity using ProBuilder and built the gameplay around physically located bridge stations and crew.
The purpose of the 3D bridge was not only visual; it created a space where narrative, ship systems, and character interaction could happen together.

sections.title: Interactable Crew
paragraphs: Crew members became interactive characters rather than portraits or abstract bridge-console representations.
The player could approach crew, receive reports, trigger conversations, and choose responses while events continued around the bridge.

sections.title: Branching Conversations
paragraphs: Dialogue could present multiple player responses and continue into different scripted actions.
This allowed mission storytelling to happen as interactive conversations between the captain and crew instead of only through static message panels.

sections.title: Narrative Inside the Simulation
paragraphs: Story interactions could occur while the bridge remained an active game environment.
Crew conversations, ship alerts, external threats, combat effects, and viewscreen events could all contribute to the same scene.

sections.title: Command & Event Runtime
paragraphs: I built a reusable runtime around GameEvent objects containing ordered command sequences.
Missions could orchestrate story and gameplay by combining commands rather than embedding every sequence directly into custom MonoBehaviour code.

sections.title: Reusable Narrative Commands
paragraphs: The command system supported a broad range of narrative and gameplay actions.

sections.title: Character-Targeted Story Actions
paragraphs: Commands could target specific bridge roles and crew members, allowing missions to coordinate characters such as Navigation, Weapons, Science, Communications, Engineering, and the Captain.

sections.title: Character Cameras
paragraphs: Dialogue sequences could temporarily shift the camera toward the speaking crew member, giving conversations a more cinematic presentation while keeping them inside the live bridge environment.

sections.title: Audio & Lip Sync
paragraphs: Dialogue commands could trigger character audio and lip-sync behavior.
The architecture integrated spoken character presentation into the same reusable command/event system as the rest of the mission.

sections.title: Animation & Expression
paragraphs: Narrative commands could control talk animations, character states, and related presentation changes as conversations played.

sections.title: Cutscene Integration
paragraphs: The runtime included cutscene support through Cinema Director, allowing larger cinematic events to be invoked from the same mission scripting architecture.

sections.title: JSON-Driven Mission Data
paragraphs: Mission and sequence data could be serialized to JSON rather than existing only as hard-coded scene logic.
This made story content more data-driven and easier to author, inspect, save, reload, and evolve.

sections.title: Live Command Authoring
paragraphs: I built live authoring tools around the command system so mission sequences could be assembled and tested directly rather than requiring a code edit for every narrative change.

sections.title: Resource Management Tools
paragraphs: The tooling also included runtime resource management for controlling what objects, environments, and content were active during a mission.

sections.title: Resource Groups
paragraphs: Resources could be organized into groups representing scene or mission states.
Commands could activate and remove these groups as the story progressed, letting missions dynamically reshape the environment.

sections.title: Performance-Level Variants
paragraphs: The resource architecture already supported multiple performance classifications so content could be enabled or excluded depending on the target performance level.

sections.title: Save, Reload & Backup
paragraphs: The authoring system supported saving and loading mission/script data as well as backup workflows, allowing narrative content to be iterated without rebuilding the entire game.

sections.title: Interactive Scripted Playthrough
paragraphs: A surviving build from this generation contains a fully interactable scripted playthrough, demonstrating that the architecture was already functional even though the recovered snapshot does not contain the complete later mission set.

sections.title: Foundation for the VR Generations
paragraphs: This pre-VR Unity version established much of the runtime architecture that later Bridge Captain VR development could build on.
The move to VR extended an existing 3D bridge, narrative, command, and resource architecture rather than starting from an empty project.

sections.title: Why Unity Changed the Project
paragraphs: Unity let me stop spending most of my effort recreating general-purpose 3D engine and editor infrastructure and instead invest that time in the actual Bridge Captain experience.
The result was the design I had wanted from the beginning: a character-driven bridge where the player could physically participate in the story.

historicalNotes: The legacy portfolio card was titled 'Bridge Captain 3D (2015)'.
Canonical public title should be 'Bridge Captain: Unity 3D'.
This card represents the pre-VR Unity generation.
The recovered Unity source appears older than the complete later mission set, but a surviving build contains a fully interactable scripted playthrough.
The project moved from a semi-3D LibGDX bridge architecture to a fully physical 3D bridge in Unity.
Bridge geometry was prototyped using ProBuilder.
The player could physically exist on the bridge with crew characters rather than interacting only through abstract bridge panels.
Crew conversations supported selectable player responses and branching story behavior.
The recovered code contains GameEvent objects composed from reusable Command sequences.
Supported command concepts include delays, dialogue, lip-synced dialogue, dialog bubbles, red alert, animations, resource groups, cutscenes, nested events, and conditions.
Commands could target specific bridge roles including Science, Communications, Weapons, Navigation, Engineering, and Captain-related characters.
Dialogue could use temporary character cameras, spoken audio, talk animations, face/presentation state changes, and portrait/dialog UI.
LipSync integration is present in the recovered source.
Cinema Director cutscene integration is present in the recovered source.
Mission/event data could be serialized to JSON under a gamescripts-style content path.

The recovered source contains live authoring infrastructure including Live Command Console, Command Manager, Command Watcher, Resource Manager, Resource Group Manager, character selection, command selection, and parameter editing.
The authoring/runtime system includes JSON save/load and backup workflows.
Resource architecture includes logical resource names, prefab paths, hierarchy relationships, optional custom loading, runtime activation/deactivation, and resource groups.
Resource groups could be dynamically added and removed to compose mission/scene states.
The resource system includes performance classifications: Low, Normal, High, LowNormal, HighNormal, and All.
The performance-level architecture is especially relevant to the later mobile VR generation, but its foundation already exists in this pre-VR Unity code.
Do not attribute every mature later VR editor feature to this specific snapshot unless independently verified; frame this version as the foundation of the later system.
The old legacy description saying Unity proved Jamie could 'never compete building my own engines' should not be preserved literally in modern public copy.
Better framing: Unity provided mature commodity 3D engine/editor infrastructure, allowing Jamie to spend his effort on game-specific interaction, narrative, tools, and content instead.
This generation established the fully 3D bridge and character-driven narrative direction that later Bridge Captain VR versions inherited.
